tracks.body:
# This Week in AI Product Management — Briefing for Vocal Media

*Framed for AI content pipelines, creator/editorial tooling, and audience automation. Six items covering frameworks, shipped-product stories, success measurement, role scoping, and one tactic to run this week.*

---

## 1. Own your evals — don't approve them
**Framework / mindset shift.** The 2026 reframe for AI PMs is that evals are your job, not something you sign off on after engineering builds them. 

The core reframe of 2026: the PM doesn't approve the eval, the PM owns it.

 This matters for Vocal because your editorial and content-generation surfaces have quality that only someone with domain and brand taste can judge — 

outsourcing the eval to engineering or QA based on acceptance criteria fails because they usually don't have the full domain expertise to spot high-impact failures beyond what's easily measurable like format.

 A related warning worth internalizing: 

validating on three happy-path examples means the demo shines, production breaks, and you find out from a churned customer or a lost deal.

**Source:** Lovelaice — https://www.lovelaice.com/resources/ai-evals-for-product-managers-complete-guide-2026

---

## 2. Product decisions, not model capability, drive AI success
**Framework with evidence.** A large study found the model is a minority of what makes an AI product win. 

BCG's 2025 analysis of 400 AI products found that model capability explained only 31% of the variance in product success; the remaining 69% was attributable to product factors — UX design, feedback loop architecture, evaluation frameworks, governance practices, and go-to-market strategy.

 For a new PM on creator tooling, this is permission to focus on the experience layer — how outputs are reviewed, edited, and fed back — rather than waiting for a better base model. The framework itself is practical: 

it evaluates products across twelve dimensions in four categories, each scored 1–5, for a composite from 12 to 60.

**Source:** thinking.inc — https://thinking.inc/en/blue-ocean/ai-native/ai-product-evaluation-framework/

---

## 3. Domain expertise beats generic AI patterns (a shipped-product story)
**Real story.** An edtech team, eSpark, learned that off-the-shelf AI search approaches broke on their real content. 

The eSpark story illustrates how domain expertise shapes AI product decisions in ways generalists would miss: when they built their teacher assistant with embeddings, queries that made sense in an educational context—like "long A" for phonics—were too generic for embeddings and matched too many irrelevant results.

 The fix was editorial, not just technical: 

the team realized they needed to add metadata to their educational content, and this is where their pedagogical expertise became critical.

 Directly relevant to Vocal — your content pipelines and audience automation will need editorial metadata and domain rules layered onto retrieval, not raw embeddings alone.
**Source:** Product Talk — https://www.producttalk.org/learning-from-8-ai-product-teams/

---

## 4. Measure two layers, and put cost in the eval
**How to measure success.** Good AI teams track outcomes and model quality together. 

Set dual success metrics: track both product outcomes (engagement, retention) and model evaluation metrics (precision, recall, latency) and understand what "good enough" looks like for each.

 A layered approach helps you avoid drowning in numbers: 

effective AI product measurement uses four layers, each serving a different purpose — think of them as a pyramid, starting at the top (user outcomes) and only digging deeper to diagnose issues.

 The most-forgotten metric is money, which matters enormously for high-volume content generation: 

if you didn't measure cost during evals, your projections are fiction — make cost part of your eval metrics, not an after-launch surprise.

**Sources:** Product School — https://productschool.com/blog/artificial-intelligence/guide-ai-product-manager · Institute of PM — https://www.institutepm.com/knowledge-hub/ai-product-metrics

---

## 5. Know which "AI PM" you actually are
**How the role is being scoped.** The title is broad, so pin down your version early. One recruiter's read: 

an AI product manager in 2026 is one of four working roles — the copilot PM who owns a customer-facing LLM surface, the AI platform PM who owns the internal model and tooling layer, the ML feature PM who ships model-powered features inside a non-AI product, or the AI ops PM who deploys AI to a non-engineering team.

 Across 12,400 postings, the emphasis is on judgment over hands-on building: 

it's a judgment-and-influence role, not a hands-on execution one — employers care more about the calls you made than the code you wrote.

 For Vocal, your work likely spans the copilot surface (creator/editorial tools) and the platform layer (content pipelines) — worth naming explicitly with your manager so scope and metrics are clear.
**Sources:** KORE1 — https://www.kore1.com/how-to-hire-ai-product-manager-2026/ · Axial Search — https://axialsearch.com/insights/ai-product-jobs

---

## 6. Tactic for this week: run error analysis on 30–50 real traces
**Apply immediately.** Before writing any new eval or metric, read your product's actual outputs and let the failures name themselves. The steps: 

gather a representative sample of traces; open code by reading each and writing a free-text note about the first thing that went wrong, with no predefined categories; then cluster similar observations into named failure categories.

 Then turn reading into a plan: 

label every trace against the taxonomy and compute failure rates per category, then for each category choose a prompt or code fix, an evaluator that catches it on future traces, or monitoring for now.

 A useful stopping rule and scope: 

no new category in the last 20 traces — around 100 total works for most apps — and once you have 30–50 notes, group them into categories.

 This is widely called the highest-value activity in AI work: 

this bottom-up process is the single highest-ROI activity in AI development — it ensures you're solving real problems, not chasing vanity metrics.

 Run it this week on one Vocal surface (e.g., an AI editorial draft or audience-automation output) and bring the failure-rate chart to your first eval review.
**Sources:** Langfuse — https://langfuse.com/blog/2025-08-29-error-analysis-to-evaluate-llm-applications · Hamel Husain — https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/why-is-error-analysis-so-important-in-llm-evals-and-how-is-it-performed.html

---

### One habit to adopt alongside these
Set a standing weekly quality check. 

Schedule weekly "eval review" sessions with your team and ask: what broke this week?

 This gives your error-analysis findings a regular home and keeps quality visible to the whole content-pipeline team.

tracks.label: AI Automations & Claude Craft
tracks.body:
# This Week in Claude & AI Automation

## 1. `/doctor prompt-audit` — lint your CLAUDE.md and skills for stale, old-model prompting

Claude Code shipped a command that scans your entire config for instructions written for older models and now working against you. 

Run /doctor prompt-audit (or /checkup prompt-audit, both work) and it scans your CLAUDE.md files, skills, agents, and slash commands for stale paths, dead commands, contradicting instructions, and prompting patterns written for older models.

 This matters because 

current Claude models follow instructions more closely and more literally than the models much of this text was written for, so the leftover text is not just wasted tokens — specific outdated instructions actively degrade behavior (over-triggering, over-planning, rigid responses in gray areas).

**Try this:** Update to Claude Code v2.1.283+, then in each project run:
```
/doctor prompt-audit
```
When it flags findings, apply the specific rewrites Anthropic's own audit reference prescribes:
- 

"CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when..." becomes "Use this tool when..."

- Replace negative constraints with positive frames: 

"Never delete files without confirmation" is a negative constraint. "Before any destructive operation, confirm with the user" is a positive frame.

- 

Remove fixed interim-update cadences and numeric output ceilings ("under 120 words") and re-express them as audience or outcome framing.

Re-run it every time a new model ships. Source: **Claude Code Changelog** — https://code.claude.com/docs/en/changelog

---

## 2. Fork subagents are now default — use `/subtask` to delegate with a warm cache

The delegation model changed and the keystrokes are not what your fingers remember. 

Claude Code fork subagents went from an opt-in experiment to the default behavior in interactive sessions with version 2.1.232.

 The payoff: 

a fresh subagent has to process its own system prompt and tool definitions from scratch on its first turn. A fork skips that: because its system prompt and tools are identical to the parent's, the underlying model can reuse the parent's already-computed prompt cache.

**Try this:** When you're deep in a session and want to spin off a side investigation without polluting your main context, run:
```
/subtask draft unit tests for the parser changes so far
```
Key gotchas to internalize: 

run a forked subagent with /subtask, which requires v2.1.212 or later. When agent view is turned off, /subtask is not available and /fork starts the forked subagent instead. Otherwise /fork copies the whole session into a new background session.

 If you want fork mode on but don't want Claude spawning forks unprompted, 

use CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=1 or =0 to override the default, and deny Agent(fork) in permissions.

 Note the ceiling: 

forks cannot spawn further forks, so deep delegation chains still need nested subagents instead.

 Source: **Claude Code Blog** — https://claudcod.com/blog/claude-code-fork-subagents/

---

## 3. Cowork scheduled tasks now run with zero devices online

Cowork's scheduled tasks graduated into genuinely unattended automation. 

Scheduled tasks run remotely, so they run on their cadence even when your computer is asleep or the Claude Desktop app is closed.

 

You describe the task once and Claude handles it on your schedule — delivering finished outputs like reports, briefings, and summaries every time,

 and 

scheduled tasks have access to the same capabilities as regular Cowork tasks, including connected tools, skills, and installed plugins.

 It's now available beyond desktop — 

on all paid plans (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise).

**Try this:** In Cowork, create a recurring task with a prompt like this (adapt the connectors to yours):

> *"Every weekday at 6:00 AM: pull the last 24 hours of Slack messages from #product and #incidents, my unread email threads flagged important, and my calendar for today. Build a one-page briefing doc grouping items by (1) needs a decision from me, (2) FYI, (3) waiting on others. For any external meeting today, add 3 bullets of recent news on that company. Draft — but do not send — reply emails for anything in category 1, and leave them as drafts for my review."*

This mirrors Anthropic's own example: 

set Monday's client prep for 6 am — Claude works through the email threads, transcripts, and recent news, builds the briefing doc, and leaves the follow-up email drafted but unsent.

 Review runs via 

"Scheduled" in the left sidebar on any surface.

 Source: **Claude Help Center** — https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13854387-schedule-recurring-tasks-in-claude-cowork

---

## 4. "Dispatch" — command your desktop's local files and apps from your phone

Distinct from remote/cloud Cowork, Dispatch is the pattern for driving your actual machine remotely. 

Dispatch creates a continuous conversation between the mobile device and the computer. Users can send commands from their phone and have Claude execute them through the Desktop machine, utilizing local files, Connectors, Plugins, and installed apps.

 The router is smart: 

software development tasks might be routed through Claude Code, while document handling, analysis, and general knowledge tasks go through Cowork.

**Try this:** Set it up once, then delegate from anywhere:
1. 

Open Cowork on either your phone or your desktop, click "Dispatch" on the left side panel.

2. 

Click "Get started" — on the next screen, toggle on access to your files and keep-your-computer-awake, then start messaging Claude within the "Dispatch" section.

3. From your phone, send something only your desktop can do, e.g. *"Pull Q3 numbers from the local spreadsheet in ~/Finance/2026-Q3.xlsx and compile a one-page summary."* 

You can hand Claude tasks that use everything on your desktop, including things you can't open on your phone.

Decision rule: 

if you want tasks to continue with the computer off, use Remote Cowork; if you need Claude to work through your computer's local files/apps, use Dispatch.

 Source: **Claude Help Center** — https://support.claude.com/en/articles/13947068-assign-tasks-from-anywhere-in-claude-cowork

---

## 5. Messages API compaction beta — compress server-side history on demand

For anyone building on the API, there's a new lever for long-running agent conversations. 

Anthropic introduced a Messages API compaction beta allowing developers to compress server-side conversation history at will. This is controlled via the new compact-2026-09-04 beta header.

**Try this:** Add the beta header to your Messages API calls to opt in:
```
anthropic-beta: compact-2026-09-04
```
Then, before shipping, 

test the compact-2026-09-04 header functionality — verify the compaction beta for your use cases and benchmark its impact on performance.

 Treat it as beta: measure output quality against your uncompacted baseline on real transcripts before wiring it into production agents. Source: **Big Hat Group / Claude Weekly** — https://www.bighatgroup.com/blog/claude-weekly-2026-09-21/

---

## 6. (Beyond Claude) Cursor's last-mile bots: Rollouts + Security Review

The broader-world pick: Cursor pushed agents past the PR and into deploy/security. 

On September 23, 2026, Cursor launched Rollouts and Security Review — one bot watches a change after it deploys, and the other reads the pull request for exploitable bugs before merge.

 

Rollouts attaches a monitor to every pull request and watches the change as it deploys, reporting change health per environment: verified healthy, regression detected, or inconclusive.

 One caveat worth knowing: they do not auto-fix your deploys — 

organizations that expected automatic rollback will be disappointed until Cursor ships that behavior.

**Try this** (Teams/Enterprise only):
1. 

Enable Rollouts from the dashboard and connect source control, your deploy system, and your telemetry provider. Rollouts starts watching on the next pull request.

2. When a PR opens, 

Rollouts reads the diff and the systems it touches, then writes a monitoring plan as a PR comment

 — read that comment; ignoring it produces weak signal coverage.
3. Enable Security Reviewer separately: 

configure Security Agents in Automations at the Security Agents page. Security Reviewer checks pull requests before merge, and Vulnerability Scanner scans the codebase at rest.

There's a trial window: 

Cursor released them on September 23 with a ten-day trial period — Teams customers receive credits covering approximately 50 code changes and Enterprise customers around 500.

 Source: **Cursor Changelog** — https://cursor.com/changelog/rollouts-and-security-reviewer

tracks.body:
The CNN-Perplexity suit is from May, not this week, so I'll set it aside in favor of fresher items. I have enough for a strong, current briefing.

# This Week in AI: A Briefing

## 1. Chinese open-weight models overtake US rivals on major developer platforms
Usage of Chinese AI models has climbed sharply in 2026, and new data shows the shift is now dramatic. 

Chinese AI models have gone from a relatively small share of usage to a majority on two major developer platforms; on OpenRouter, they accounted for 57%-67% of tokens used in the week of Sept. 14, up from 6%-13% earlier.

 The driver is cost and improving quality: 

the most advanced US models lead most benchmarks, but Chinese companies like DeepSeek, Z.ai and Alibaba have released new models with major performance gains in tasks such as coding.

 This matters because model choice for many companies is now driven by price-performance rather than national origin, and Washington worries the trend could pull countries into a Chinese technology sphere. It's directly relevant to any media firm evaluating which models to build on.
**Region:** China / Global · **Source:** CNBC — https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/26/china-ai-global-adoption.html

## 2. Trump and Xi discuss AI at summit; two governments set up a safety hotline
AI was a central topic when the US and Chinese leaders met this week, reflecting how quickly the technology has risen up the geopolitical agenda. 

After wrapping up a summit with Xi Jinping, Trump said he would not back off the pursuit of AI dominance over China, but the two countries did agree to set up a channel for handling AI-related safety incidents.

 The framing itself became a point of friction: 

the White House said Trump and Xi agreed to refer to AI as "super intelligence" going forward, but the Chinese government's statement continued to use the term "artificial intelligence."

 China publicly struck a more cooperative note, with 

Xi saying the two countries "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more" in AI, that they can exchange views on risks and jointly prevent misuse, and that "AI must be kept under human control."

 The safety-incident channel is a modest but notable first step toward superpower coordination on AI risk.
**Region:** US / China · **Source:** Fox News — https://www.foxnews.com/live-news/ai-leaders-trump-xi-xinping-state-dinner-white-house

## 3. Alibaba unveils "China's most powerful AI chip" as Beijing pushes self-reliance
Ahead of the Trump-Xi meeting, Alibaba made a hardware statement aimed at reducing dependence on US technology. 

China's Alibaba unveiled new AI chip technologies and plans for more powerful models on Tuesday, including what it said was China's most powerful AI chip, days ahead of the leaders' meeting.

 

CEO Eddie Wu said the new Zhenwu V900 chip can deliver three times the performance of the company's previous generation Zhenwu M890 chip.

 The context is US export controls that have blocked China from buying Nvidia's top chips: 

frontier AI training in China often relies on Nvidia chips, analysts say, but Chinese-designed chips are gaining ground as Nvidia has been blocked from selling its most powerful chips there.

 Analysts remain skeptical the gap is closing fast, but the timing gave Beijing leverage as export-control talks continue.
**Region:** China · **Source:** ABC News — https://abcnews.com/International/wireStory/chinas-alibaba-unveils-new-powerful-chip-ambitious-ai-136641611

## 4. Europe moves to loosen its own AI Act as enforcement begins
The EU is rethinking parts of the landmark law even as its first major provisions take hold, a tension directly relevant to media companies operating in Europe. 

The EU is giving companies more time to adapt to its new AI regulations, but experts and MEPs say they regret the rowback on rules adopted just a year ago.

 A further easing is on the way: 

a digital simplification package will likely ease the burden on AI companies, Tech Commissioner Henna Virkkunen told Euronews.

 At the same time, the law is adding new prohibitions — 

the European Parliament and Council are outlawing "nudifier apps," with a ban from 2 December targeting AI systems for sexual deepfakes and users creating false intimate content of real people without consent.

 For publishers, the direction of travel matters: transparency and content-disclosure rules shape how AI-generated media must be labeled across the EU market.
**Region:** EU · **Source:** Euronews — https://www.euronews.com/tag/ai-act

## 5. Media licensing and litigation intensify: UMG, ElevenLabs, and a Danish standoff with OpenAI
The market for paying publishers and rights-holders for AI use keeps splitting into deals and lawsuits — the core story for any media business. On the deal side, 

Universal Music and ElevenLabs signed a multi-year AI deal and will launch a licensed fan remix platform,

 part of a broader wave in which 

news publishers dominate the licensing economy, with news/journalism accounting for 48 deals — far ahead of music/audio and images/video — implying AI companies value constantly refreshed, real-time text, as the market shifts from "training data" to "live access."

 On the conflict side, publishers abroad are turning to courts: 

a Danish rights body said it tried to negotiate with OpenAI to comply with Danish copyright law and secure a "fair exchange of value," but that OpenAI "declined to enter into meaningful negotiations" and refused mediation, making court proceedings "inevitable."

 The takeaway: large publishers are negotiating live-content feeds while smaller and non-US players increasingly litigate to establish leverage.
**Region:** EU / Global · **Source:** Press Gazette — https://pressgazette.co.uk/platforms/news-publisher-ai-deals-lawsuits-openai-google/

*Note: A few widely circulated items this week — such as reports of Nvidia acquiring Hugging Face and a rapid run of frontier model releases (OpenAI's GPT-6 line, Anthropic's Claude 5.5 family) — appear in trade coverage but warrant independent confirmation before you treat the specifics as settled.*

# Cross-Spectrum Political Briefing — Week of September 22–28, 2026

Four stories driving the final stretch before the November 3 midterms. For each: a neutral factual anchor, then progressive, neutral, and conservative reads.

---

## 1. Supreme Court revives Trump's SAVE voter-citizenship database

**What actually happened (factual anchor):** 

On September 25, the Supreme Court, divided 6-3 along ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request from the government after lower courts ruled the administration's changes to the SAVE database were likely unlawful.

 

The decision clears the way for the administration to use the revamped SAVE system to check voter rolls for noncitizens.

 

Federal law bans states from "systematically" removing voters from rolls within 90 days of a federal election,

 so the practical effect on the 2026 election is limited. SAVE was originally created by Congress in 1986 to verify immigration status for benefits programs, and was expanded to pull in Social Security records and allow bulk checks.

**PROGRESSIVE**
*Mother Jones — reporting/analysis — https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2026/09/supreme-court-save-database/*
The left frames this as the Court blessing an unreliable tool that risks disenfranchising eligible citizens on a false premise. The piece points to a track record of debunked fraud claims: 

following Trump's July speech, DHS claimed 15,903 noncitizens were registered to vote in Nevada; a month later DHS confirmed the number was actually "just 185 potential noncitizens," and Nevada officials subsequently confirmed the number was actually zero.

 Progressives stress the database's error rate and that 

the impact could be muted because the National Voter Registration Act precludes states from removing voters ninety days before an election, making it "too late for States to use SAVE for systematic voter-list maintenance in advance of the 2026 elections," as Justice Jackson wrote.

**NEUTRAL**
*Reuters (via U.S. News) — wire reporting — https://www.usnews.com/news/politics/articles/2026-09-25/supreme-court-restores-trumps-mass-voter-verification-system*
Straight reporting lays out both sides' stakes. 

The Supreme Court revived an expanded immigration database that Trump's administration said aims to combat voting by noncitizens but critics contend could disenfranchise eligible voters.

 

The justices granted the Justice Department's request to block a judge's order that had stopped state officials from using Social Security numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of citizenship status against federal records.

 

The ruling allows the federal government to use the database for now, but questions remain about its accuracy and how quickly states can act before the November election.

**CONSERVATIVE**
*American Greatness — reporting/opinion — https://amgreatness.com/2026/09/26/supreme-court-clears-trump-administration-to-expand-voter-citizenship-checks/*
The right frames this as a win for election integrity and a proper check on judicial overreach. 

The Court handed the administration a victory, allowing federal officials to work with states using an expanded citizenship-verification database; the 6-3 ruling permits state officials to use the modified SAVE program to verify citizenship of registered voters, incorporating Social Security records and allowing batch checks.

 Conservatives cite the administration's argument that the tool is a service, not a purge: 

"SAVE does not disqualify any voter; instead, it merely notifies the States whether the federal government can confirm citizenship," Solicitor General Sauer wrote.

**Fact check for the reader:** The core conservative claim that this stops widespread noncitizen voting rests on a factual weak point. 

Noncitizen voting is extremely rare, all states are already required to conduct voter roll maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify noncitizens who accidentally make it onto rolls.

 The database's documented error rate is also real and demonstrable: 

advocacy groups cited a Travis County, Texas, election official who said 25% of the system's noncitizen matches there involved people who had already proven their U.S. citizenship, and news reports finding that at least 81% of the system's responses in St. Louis County, Missouri, were erroneous.

---

## 2. Supreme Court blocks Missouri's GOP-drawn congressional map — for the third time

**What actually happened (factual anchor):** 

For the third time in September, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri from using a new congressional map that favors Republicans, ending a legal fight that created major confusion around November's midterm elections in the state.

 

Congressional elections will be held in the district lines drawn in 2022, and the court reversed Secretary of State Denny Hoskins's decision that a referendum on the plan was not allowed.

 Voters will decide the map's future via referendum in November. The map was redrawn mid-decade in 2025 and would have dismantled a Democratic-leaning district.

**PROGRESSIVE**
*Missouri Independent — reporting — https://missouriindependent.com/2026/09/03/missouri-supreme-court-blocks-gerrymandered-congressional-map-orders-referendum-vote/*
Progressives frame this as voters defeating a partisan power grab. 

The court ruled unanimously that Missourians will vote on the "gerrymandered" congressional map "muscled through" the Legislature in 2025, putting a congressional plan before voters for the first time since 1922.

 The left emphasizes the citizen mobilization: 

Rep. Emanuel Cleaver said "more than 305,000 Missourians demanded a say," and that despite "the cynical and deeply shameful attempt to silence" voters, "the people fought back and won" and "democracy prevails."

**NEUTRAL**
*NBC News — reporting — https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/missouri-supreme-court-rules-gop-drawn-map-cant-used-november-election-rcna595688*
Wire-style reporting states the facts and the stakes without loaded framing. 

The Missouri Supreme Court ruled the state's redrawn congressional map cannot be used in the midterms, dealing a blow to Republicans, and that a referendum on whether the state can use the map must be on the November ballot, meaning fall elections take place under previous district lines.

 

Missouri redrew its map in 2025 at the behest of President Trump; People Not Politicians Missouri gathered more than 300,000 signatures to force a veto referendum; and while the group exceeded the requirement, Secretary of State Hoskins refused to certify it, saying it was unconstitutional.

**CONSERVATIVE**
*Missouri Attorney General Catherine Hanaway (via NBC News) — official statement — https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/missouri-supreme-court-rules-gop-drawn-map-cant-used-november-election-rcna595688*
The conservative argument centers on timing and procedure — that overturning a map after a primary is unprecedented and disruptive. 

Hanaway vowed to appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, arguing "never before in American history has a court overturned a congressional map after a primary and before a general election."

 The GOP also argued the ruling itself creates chaos: 

Hanaway said "we are confident that the federal courts will not allow every Missouri voter to be disenfranchised — which is what today's decision does."

*Note on balance:* Both sides used "disenfranchise." The underlying dispute is genuinely one of legal interpretation — 

the Missouri Constitution does not specifically say a referendum petition can be used for a congressional redistricting law, but the state Supreme Court ruled that a provision allowing a referendum on "any act" of the Legislature encompasses congressional redistricting.

---

## 3. Taxpayer-funded pro-Trump ads spark bipartisan backlash

**What actually happened (factual anchor):** 

Television advertisements with a pro-Trump message and paid for by the U.S. government are expanding ahead of November's midterms, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the campaign complies with federal restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity.

 

The White House is airing TV ads promoting Trump and his policies that say they are "Paid for by the U.S. Government."

 

One ad is nearly identical to an ad put out by Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, which he posted to Truth Social in January 2024.

 The White House calls them public service announcements.

**PROGRESSIVE**
*MS NOW / Rachel Maddow Blog — opinion — https://www.ms.now/rachel-maddow-show/maddowblog/trump-propaganda-ad-campaign-psa-congress-pushback*
The left frames these flatly as government-funded campaign propaganda mislabeled as public service. The piece argues a real PSA advances public safety or health, while 

the 30-second ad, launched as early voting opens, "looks like a campaign commercial because it is: The spot is filled with images and video clips of Trump and his campaign slogans."

 It concludes that 

the ad serves no purpose other than to glorify the president, and that the administration began using public funds to air political propaganda.

**NEUTRAL**
*CNBC — reporting — https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/27/trump-government-funded-ads-midterms.html*
Straight reporting describes the ads and the legal question without endorsing either side. 

One ad, backed by music repeating "love me," features images of Trump saying "America will never be a communist country," with campaign talking points like "largest tax cuts in history" flashing over the screen.

 

The White House compared the ads to previous administrations' PSAs about Medicare, Obamacare and Covid-19 vaccination, saying its commercials "are very clearly not campaign ads."

**CONSERVATIVE / BIPARTISAN CRITICISM**
*The Washington Times — reporting — https://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2026/sep/28/white-house-faces-bipartisan-backlash-stylish-taxpayer-funded-ads/*
Notably, this story is not split cleanly on partisan lines — a conservative-leaning outlet reports the criticism as bipartisan.
